body_markdown:
## How to choose workplace management software


Start with the problems you have today: people can't find a desk, rooms get double-booked, nobody knows who is coming in, or leadership wants to know if the office is the right size. Then check each tool against these points.


### Where people book


A booking tool only works if people use it. Check whether people can book inside the apps they already have open all day, such as Microsoft Teams or Slack, as well as on the web and on their phone. Ask to see the actual booking flow in your chat tool, not just a logo on an integrations page.


### What people can book


Desks are the starting point. List everything else you want people to book: meeting rooms, car parking, lockers or anything else that runs short. For meeting rooms, check where the booking happens (inside the tool, inside your calendar app or both) and whether it syncs with your calendars.


### Floor plans


A live floor plan helps people pick a desk near their team and see who is in. Ask who builds the floor plans, how long changes take and whether you can upload your existing drawings.


### Rules and approvals


As more people come in, you will want some control. Look for team areas, approval steps for certain desks or rooms, and limits on how many bookings one person can hold.


### Attendance and space reports


Reports are often what justifies the purchase. You want to see which days are busy, which areas sit empty and how attendance changes over time, so you can decide whether you have the right amount of space.


### Pricing model and published prices


Vendors charge in three main ways: per user (every employee who can book), per space or resource (every bookable desk, room or parking space) or per plan or site (a flat monthly fee with limits). Some add a platform fee or a monthly minimum. Prefer vendors that publish prices, and model the cost on your own headcount and space count, not the example on the pricing page.


### Setup


Ask who does the setup work, whether the vendor can bring across your current setup and whether you can start small. Running a new tool on one floor alongside your current one is the lowest-risk way to test it.

## The 8 tools in more detail


### 1. Officely: our pick for Teams-first mid-size companies


We make Officely, so treat this as our view. People book desks, meeting rooms and car parking in Microsoft Teams or on the web, and see who is in on a live floor plan. Admins set booking rules, approvals and caps, and get attendance and space-use reports. There is an API for your own workflows, and an MCP server lets AI assistants work with Officely. A new version for Slack is coming soon.


**Price** : one plan with every feature, at $2 per bookable desk, room or parking space a month billed annually, or $2.50 billed monthly. The minimum is $500 a month. You pay for spaces, not headcount, so the bill doesn't grow when you hire people who rarely come in.


**Setup** : setup is assisted, and you can start with one office or floor while your current tool keeps running.


**Where it falls short** :


- Visitor management covers invites, sign-in on arrival, host alerts and a Reception role, but there's no badge printing or NDA signing. If your front desk needs those, look at a dedicated visitor tool such as Envoy.
- Meeting rooms are booked in Teams or on the web and sync with your calendar. You can't book an Officely room from inside Outlook.
- On annual billing, the $500 monthly minimum covers 250 bookable spaces at $2 each (200 at $2.50 billed monthly). An office with fewer than about 250 desks, rooms and parking spaces pays the minimum, so smaller offices will find cheaper options in this list.
- Slack booking isn't available yet.


See the full[office management](https://getofficely.com/office-management) features and[pricing](https://getofficely.com/pricing) .


### 2. deskbird


deskbird is a desk and room booking app for hybrid teams, with a mobile app and a web app. It publishes clear per-user prices, which makes budgeting simple for smaller companies.


**Price** : the Business plan is $3.75 per active user a month billed annually, or $4.75 billed monthly.


**Worth checking** : per-user pricing grows with headcount, including people who rarely come in. Model the cost on everyone who needs access. See[Officely vs deskbird](https://getofficely.com/officely-vs-deskbird) .


### 3. Tactic


Tactic covers desk and room booking and helps teams plan days in the office together. It doesn't publish a flat price list. Instead, an estimator prices your setup per resource.


**Price** : Tactic's own example is $3,600 to $4,800 a year for 100 desks at one site.


**Worth checking** : run your real numbers through the estimator, especially if you have more than one site. See[Officely vs Tactic](https://getofficely.com/officely-vs-tactic) .


### 4. OfficeRnD Workplace


OfficeRnD Workplace covers desk and room booking and office planning for hybrid teams.


**Price** : the Start plan is from $99 a month billed annually, for up to 150 users, with per-resource fees on top.


**Worth checking** : how the per-resource fees add up once you count every desk and room. See[Officely vs OfficeRnD](https://getofficely.com/officely-vs-officernd) .


### 5. Robin


Robin is a workplace platform built around office maps, with desk and room booking and space analytics. It sells to larger organisations through a sales-led process.


**Price** : quote only. Robin's pricing page says it is aimed at companies with 500+ employees, billed annually.


**Worth checking** : with no published price, plan time for a quote and an annual commitment. See[Officely vs Robin](https://getofficely.com/officely-vs-robin) .


### 6. Envoy


Envoy is best known for visitor management and also sells desk and room booking. If your front desk handles lots of guests, it is the obvious one to look at.


**Price** : desk booking (Envoy calls it Reservations) costs $5 per bookable resource a month, billed annually. The platform fee is extra. Visitors has a free Basic plan.


**Worth checking** : products are priced separately, and the platform fee sits on top. See[Officely vs Envoy](https://getofficely.com/officely-vs-envoy) .


### 7. Skedda


Skedda is a space booking tool used for desks, meeting rooms and other shared spaces. Because it charges per space, the price stays the same when headcount changes.


**Price** : US plans start at $249 a month for 35 spaces, billed annually.


**Worth checking** : how the price steps up as you add spaces. See[Officely vs Skedda](https://getofficely.com/officely-vs-skedda) .


### 8. Archie


Archie offers desk and room booking for hybrid and flexible offices on flat monthly plans.


**Price** : Starter starts at $159 a month and Pro starts at $249 a month.


**Worth checking** : what each plan includes and where its limits sit before you outgrow it.


## Per user, per space or per site: what you will actually pay


The pricing model matters as much as the headline price. Here is an example using list prices, checked November 2026. Take a company with 600 staff and 500 bookable spaces: 400 desks, 30 meeting rooms and 70 parking spaces.


- **Officely** (per space): 500 spaces at $2 is $1,000 a month billed annually, covering desks, rooms and parking.
- **deskbird Business** (per active user): 600 active users at $3.75 is $2,250 a month billed annually, if all 600 count as active.
- **Envoy desk booking** (per resource): 400 desks at $5 is $2,000 a month billed annually, before the platform fee and before rooms or parking.


For a small office the picture flips. A team of 100 people with 60 desks would pay $375 a month on deskbird Business if all 100 count as active, while Officely would charge its $500 minimum.


These are list prices only. Discounts, add-ons and fees change the real number, so ask each vendor to price your actual setup.


## Frequently asked questions


### What is the difference between workplace management software and office management software?


They mostly mean the same thing today: software to book desks, rooms and parking and to understand how the office is used. "Office management software" is the older term and sometimes includes general admin tools. "Workplace management software" more often means hybrid booking, floor plans and space data.


### Is workplace management software the same as an IWMS?


No. An[integrated workplace management system (IWMS)](https://getofficely.com/blog/what-is-an-integrated-workplace-management-system) is a heavier facilities and real-estate tool that covers leases, maintenance, assets and portfolio planning. Workplace management software focuses on the day-to-day: booking, attendance and space use. Many companies only need the second.


### How is workplace management software priced?


Usually per user, per bookable space or resource, or as a flat monthly plan. Some vendors add a platform fee or a monthly minimum, and some only give quotes. Per-space pricing tends to suit companies with more people than desks, while per-user or flat plans can be cheaper for smaller offices.


### Can I book desks and rooms inside Microsoft Teams?


Yes, with tools built for it. Officely lets people book desks, meeting rooms and parking inside Microsoft Teams and on the web. Other vendors offer Teams apps or integrations too, so ask each one to show the booking flow inside Teams during the demo.


### Does workplace management software include visitor management?


Some tools include it and some don't. Envoy is best known for visitor management. Officely includes visitor invites, sign-in on arrival and host alerts in its one plan, but it doesn't print badges or collect NDA signatures, so a front desk that needs those would still use a dedicated visitor tool.


### Can we try a new tool without replacing our current one?


Most vendors offer a demo or trial. With Officely, you can start with one office or floor alongside your current tool, with assisted setup, before deciding on the rest.
